DESCRIPTION: Unique identifier of one scheduled execution request; the grain of the Data Grid
LONG_DESCRIPTION: This is the primary key of the scheduler request table and the grain of every row in the Data Grid. One RequestID represents a single attempt to run a job at a point in time, so a job that runs nightly produces one RequestID per night. Use it when reporting an individual run to the scheduling team, because JobID alone identifies the definition rather than the occurrence.

DESCRIPTION: Identifier of the job definition this request executed; the join key to the Job table
LONG_DESCRIPTION: This identifies the job definition rather than the run. It is the join key between View_Scheduler_PBI_Dashboard and the Job table, and it is the key used by the Job Notes feature, so a note recorded against a JobID is visible against every subsequent execution of that job. A JobID that appears with many RequestIDs in a short window usually indicates retries.

DESCRIPTION: Human-readable name of the job. EDITABLE: can be corrected in place from the Data Grid
LONG_DESCRIPTION: This is the operator-facing name of the job and the label most people recognise in handover notes and incident tickets. It is the one field in this view that DMW can update: clicking the cell opens an editor that writes the change back through the dmw_update_jobname stored process. Because the name is used in conversation rather than as a key, correcting a misleading name has real operational value and no downstream referential risk.

DESCRIPTION: Scheduling cadence recorded on the request, such as Daily, Weekly or AdHoc
LONG_DESCRIPTION: This records the cadence under which the request was raised. It is denormalised onto the request so that historical runs retain the cadence in force at the time, which may differ from the cadence currently defined on the Job record. When the two disagree, the Job table holds the current intent and this column holds what actually happened.

DESCRIPTION: Current execution state of the request; the primary field for triage and the dashboard KPIs
LONG_DESCRIPTION: This is the single most important column for operational triage and the field the Dashboard and Visualize tabs group by. Values distinguish work that completed from work that failed, is still running, or is queued. Treat the vocabulary as data rather than assumption: filter on the values actually present before writing any rule, because a status that is absent from your sample is not necessarily absent from the system.

DESCRIPTION: Account or process that raised the request; distinguishes scheduled runs from manual intervention
LONG_DESCRIPTION: This records the identity that raised the execution request, which may be the scheduler service account for an automatic run or a named person for a manual one. It is the fastest way to separate routine automated activity from human intervention, and a sudden rise in manually raised requests for a given job is usually a sign that the automated path is failing quietly.

DESCRIPTION: Timestamp the request entered the scheduler queue; the start of the elapsed-time clock
LONG_DESCRIPTION: This is when the request was placed on the queue, not when execution began. It anchors every elapsed-time and backlog calculation in DMW. A widening gap between this timestamp and LastUpdateDatetime across many jobs indicates queue congestion rather than a problem with any individual job.

DESCRIPTION: Timestamp the request record was last modified; used to detect stalled runs
LONG_DESCRIPTION: This moves every time the scheduler touches the record, so it is the best available proxy for liveness. A request that is still in a running state but whose last update is hours old is stalled rather than slow, and that distinction determines whether you wait or intervene.

DESCRIPTION: Timestamp execution finished. NULL means the run has not yet completed
LONG_DESCRIPTION: This is populated only when the run reaches a terminal state, so a NULL value is meaningful rather than missing: it identifies work that is still in flight. The Dashboard counts NULL values as 'not yet completed'. Subtracting RequestedDatetime from this column gives true end-to-end duration including queue wait.

DESCRIPTION: Free-text outcome message from the job; the first place to look when a run fails
LONG_DESCRIPTION: This carries whatever the job itself reported on completion, typically a short success acknowledgement or the text of the error that stopped it. It is unstructured and its wording varies by job, so it is better suited to reading during triage than to filtering or aggregation. Paste its content into the Ask DMW assistant to find the matching runbook passage.

DESCRIPTION: Path to the scheduler-level log for this run
LONG_DESCRIPTION: This points to the log written by the scheduler about the run as a whole: dispatch, queueing, and the outcome it observed. It answers whether the job was started correctly, as distinct from what the program did once running. Check this before the program log when a run appears not to have started at all.

DESCRIPTION: Path to the SAS program log produced by the executing program
LONG_DESCRIPTION: This points to the SAS log written by the program itself and is where errors, warnings and step timings actually appear. It is the file to open for any failure where the scheduler successfully started the work. The Visualizations tab is built from these logs once they have been scanned by scanFileSystem.ps1.

DESCRIPTION: Identifier correlating this run to its entries in the central logging store
LONG_DESCRIPTION: This correlates the request to detailed entries in the central logging subsystem, allowing a run to be traced across systems when the log files themselves have been archived or rotated away. It is primarily of use to the platform team rather than to day-to-day triage.

DESCRIPTION: Configured timeout for the run. CONFIRM THE UNIT before using it in any calculation
LONG_DESCRIPTION: This is the limit after which the scheduler abandons the run. The unit is not self-evident from the column name and is not documented in the source view, so confirm whether it is expressed in seconds or minutes with the scheduling team before using it in any arithmetic. A duration comparison built on the wrong unit will be wrong by a factor of sixty and will look plausible.

DESCRIPTION: Populated when the run was raised ad hoc rather than on schedule; NULL for scheduled runs
LONG_DESCRIPTION: A non-null value marks the run as an out-of-band execution rather than a scheduled one. Counting non-null values by job over time is a direct measure of how much manual intervention a job requires, which is often a better candidate for automation work than the raw failure count.

DESCRIPTION: Populated when the run raised an alert; links the run to the alerting subsystem
LONG_DESCRIPTION: A non-null value indicates the run generated an alert through the monitoring subsystem. Comparing alerted runs against failed runs exposes two separate problems: failures that never alerted, and alerts that fired on runs that actually succeeded.

DESCRIPTION: Time of day the job is scheduled to run
LONG_DESCRIPTION: This is the clock time at which the job is due to start under its normal schedule. Comparing it against RequestedDatetime shows schedule drift, where jobs are consistently entering the queue later than intended because an upstream dependency is slow.

DESCRIPTION: Day of week the job runs, for weekly cadences
LONG_DESCRIPTION: This applies to weekly schedules and is null or ignored for other cadences. It is useful for explaining why a job that appears to have 'stopped running' simply has not reached its scheduled day.

DESCRIPTION: Day of month the job runs, for monthly cadences
LONG_DESCRIPTION: This applies to monthly schedules. Jobs with a day of month at or near the end of the month warrant attention because they interact with month-end processing load and with the business-day rules below.

DESCRIPTION: Whether the job is restricted to business days
LONG_DESCRIPTION: When set, the job is confined to business days and will not run at a weekend. This is the first thing to check when a daily job appears to have missed a run: a Saturday gap is correct behaviour rather than a failure.

DESCRIPTION: Whether the job runs on recognised holidays
LONG_DESCRIPTION: This governs behaviour on the holiday calendar. Together with RunsOnBusinessDay and RunOnNextValidWorkday it determines what happens when a scheduled date is not a working day, and the three must be read together to predict the actual run date.

DESCRIPTION: Month the job runs, for annual or quarterly cadences
LONG_DESCRIPTION: This applies to annual and quarterly schedules. Jobs carrying a value here run rarely, which makes them the ones most likely to fail unnoticed because nobody is watching on the day.

DESCRIPTION: Numeric component of a recurring interval; read together with IntervalType
LONG_DESCRIPTION: This is the numeric part of a repeating interval and is meaningless on its own. An Interval of 15 means nothing until IntervalType tells you whether that is fifteen minutes, hours or days. Always read the pair together.

DESCRIPTION: Unit that qualifies Interval, such as minutes, hours or days
LONG_DESCRIPTION: This supplies the unit for the Interval column. The pair defines sub-daily recurrence for jobs that run more often than once a day, which are the jobs most likely to generate queue congestion when an upstream system slows down.

DESCRIPTION: Earliest time the job is permitted to start
LONG_DESCRIPTION: This is the opening of the permitted execution window. A job that is ready before this time waits rather than running. When a job appears stuck in a queued state, check the window before assuming a scheduler fault.

DESCRIPTION: Latest time the job is permitted to start or continue
LONG_DESCRIPTION: This closes the permitted execution window. A long-running job that crosses this boundary may be abandoned rather than completing, which presents as an unexplained failure late in a batch cycle.

DESCRIPTION: Date from which the job definition is active
LONG_DESCRIPTION: Before this date the definition exists but is not scheduled. It is useful when reconciling a job that is present in the catalogue yet has no run history: the definition may simply not have taken effect yet.

DESCRIPTION: Date after which the job definition is no longer active; NULL means open-ended
LONG_DESCRIPTION: After this date the definition stops being scheduled. A NULL value means the job runs indefinitely. Populating this column is the clean way to retire a job, and jobs with a past effective end should be excluded from failure reporting rather than counted as missing.

DESCRIPTION: Timestamp of the most recent execution recorded against the job definition
LONG_DESCRIPTION: This is maintained on the definition rather than the request and gives the quickest answer to 'when did this job last run at all'. A last run date far in the past on an enabled, in-effect job is a strong signal of a silently broken schedule.

DESCRIPTION: Whether the job definition is currently active in the scheduler
LONG_DESCRIPTION: A disabled job produces no requests. This is the first column to check when a job has stopped appearing, because a disabled schedule looks identical to a broken one from the request side. Confirm who disabled it and when before re-enabling.

DESCRIPTION: Whether a run falling on a non-working day is deferred to the next working day
LONG_DESCRIPTION: When set, a scheduled date that falls on a weekend or holiday is deferred rather than skipped. This is why a run can legitimately appear on a date that matches none of the schedule columns, and it is a common source of confusion when reconciling expected against actual runs.

DESCRIPTION: Business area the job belongs to, such as DME, Part A or Part B
LONG_DESCRIPTION: This attributes the job to a business area and is the natural grouping for reporting scheduler health to business owners rather than to the platform team. It is also the dimension that makes a failure count meaningful, since one area's overnight batch may dwarf another's in volume.

DESCRIPTION: Category of work performed, such as extract, report or load
LONG_DESCRIPTION: This classifies the kind of work the job performs. Grouping failures by type usually localises a problem faster than grouping by name, because a cluster of failing extracts points at a source system while a cluster of failing reports points at the reporting platform.

DESCRIPTION: Whether the job must start at precisely the scheduled time rather than when resources allow
LONG_DESCRIPTION: When set, the job is expected to start at the exact scheduled time rather than being released when capacity is available. Jobs with this flag are the ones whose queue delays matter most, because a late start is itself a breach rather than a tolerable variation.
